reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is presented as a screen-recorded tutorial on configuring a Google AdWords campaign, including audience, keywords, bidding, and draft ad text. The Norton activation and live-support language appears within campaign setup, alongside discussion of a platform policy warning and a plan to address fake clicks. The material does not establish that the draft was published, that the advertiser was unauthorized, or that a completed transaction or confirmed victim-directed solicitation occurred.

opening.argument: The material links a branded support promise to concrete user actions. The proposed ad says “Activate Norton” and presents “Norton experts available,” while its description directs the viewer to install the product, enter a product key, and call live support. The campaign is explicitly designed to generate calls, not merely explain advertising theory: the title is about generating Norton tech-support calls, and the speaker calls the keyword “the most important keyword in this project.” That combination presents access to Norton assistance as the reason to respond to the ad and provide information or make contact. The evidence does not establish that the advertiser is Norton or that the destination is authorized, so the branded support promise and requested action should be treated as a scam solicitation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a tutorial does not resolve the central issue: the tutorial is specifically about producing Norton-support calls and supplies the proposed solicitation language. A draft ad can still reveal the intended deceptive pathway; publication or a completed victim transaction is not required to identify the solicitation itself. The policy warning also shows the ad required correction before approval, which undermines treating it as ordinary, established support outreach.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted copy shows only a proposed ad draft, not a completed scam or an unauthorized Norton identity. The video explains campaign fields and even addresses a punctuation-and-symbols policy warning: “that needs to be removed.” Neither the title nor the draft establishes that viewers were actually contacted, that a product key was obtained, or that any reward or asset was acquired. The argument turns an unlaunched configuration example into a proven solicitation.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: an unusually large proposed daily budget, expensive bidding for Norton-related keywords, a support ad that asks for a product key and a live call, and a destination that is visibly separate from the Norton wording in the ad. The speaker says the budget is “$25,000 per day,” later describes a bid of 135 per click, and the preview says “Install & Activate Your Product Now Enter Your Product Key Call Live Support.” The scale and urgency make the campaign look engineered to capture high-value support inquiries rather than provide neutral education. The evidence does not verify Norton authorization or explain why a user should provide a product key to this advertiser, so these signals collectively support treating the offer as deceptive.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense recasts the figures as ordinary configuration, but the combination remains significant: a $25,000 daily setting, a high per-click bid, and support language requesting a product key. The preview also shows the ad beside a non-Norton-looking landing-page address, while the material never establishes authorization. A platform warning is not reassurance; it confirms the proposed wording raised compliance concerns.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The numbers are settings in a campaign walkthrough, not evidence of money taken from viewers or of a promised return. The speaker expressly says the budget “doesn't mean that I have to spend it” and describes changing it for analysis. The ad preview is likewise not proof that anyone was solicited or that the destination was unauthorized. The policy warning concerns punctuation and symbols, not fraud.

opening.argument: The apparent educational framing functions as promotion because every operational step serves a commercial funnel for Norton-support calls. The title promises a method to generate those calls, the description says the video explores a PPC campaign for “inbound calls/Norton Support/Tech support,” and the speaker supplies ready-to-use copy: “Activate Norton,” “Norton experts available,” and instructions to call live support. The closing invitation goes beyond teaching Google Ads, offering to build campaign websites and provide help. This is therefore promotional steering toward a support-contact pathway, with Norton branding used to attract the audience, rather than a detached technology demonstration.

citations.quote: How to Generate Norton Tech Support Calls Using Google Adwords Campaign
This video explores how to setup a PPC Google Campaign for inbound calls/Norton Support/Tech support and Services
activate Norton experts available
if you guys want to campaign website to be built for any type of campaign or campaign please do call me

rebuttal.rebuttal: The “tutorial” label describes the format, not the function. The speaker is not merely reviewing Google Ads; he is constructing a live-looking Norton support promotion, selecting Norton keywords and writing the call-to-action text. The closing offer to build campaign websites further shows a commercial objective. Explaining campaign mechanics does not neutralize the branded funnel being demonstrated.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The same facts are consistent with a business tutorial about advertising services, which is exactly what the description says: setting up a PPC campaign while complying with AdWords policies. Offering campaign-building help is not evidence of a scam, and drafting an ad does not prove the speaker represented himself as Norton or that anyone was directed to pay or surrender information. The educational role remains supported by the step-by-step campaign configuration.
